specAnchors.text: know that most metals are extracted from ores found in the Earth’s crust and that unreactive metals are often found as the uncombined element

primer.text: From Reactivity Series you know that metals differ hugely in how readily they react. That difference decides where each metal is found and how it is won back from its compounds. This note covers the ores of the Earth's crust, why some metals sit in the ground as elements, and the routes used to extract the rest.

modules.title: Sources of Metals: Ores of the Crust
modules.opening: Most metals are locked away in the Earth's crust as compounds, mixed into rocks called ores. An ore is a rock that holds enough of the metal to make extraction worthwhile. Because many ores are oxides, winning the metal means removing its oxygen, which makes extraction a reduction process.
keyPoints: The crust holds both native metals and metal compounds, gold and copper among them.
Many useful metals sit chemically joined to other elements inside rocks called ores.
An ore is a rock that contains enough metal to make extraction worthwhile.
Metals are extracted from their ores by electrolysis, in a blast furnace, or by reaction with a more reactive material.
Oxide ores such as haematite and bauxite give up their oxygen during extraction, so the process is reduction.

low.restatement: Most metals are dug up as compounds in ores rather than as pure elements. If the ore is an oxide, extracting the metal means stripping the oxygen away, which is a reduction.
low.analogy: Imagine coins baked into a loaf of bread: the metal is there, but effort is needed to separate it, and only a rich enough loaf is worth the baking.
low.examPointer: Know the two named ores: haematite for iron and bauxite for aluminium, and be ready to define an ore in one sentence.

medium.restatement: A metal's compounds in the crust are its ores, and only rock rich enough in the metal pays for extraction. Because the common ores are oxides, the extraction step removes oxygen, so any chemistry that strips oxygen from a metal compound is described as reduction of that compound.
medium.analogy: Think of rust scraped off an old bike: the shiny metal underneath appears only once the oxygen is taken away, which is the same job a furnace does on an ore.
medium.examPointer: Exam hints stress direction: one metal can only remove oxygen from another metal's compound if it is the more reactive of the two.

modules.title: Unreactive Metals Found Uncombined
modules.opening: Unreactive metals are different: they are so chemically stable that they often occur as the uncombined element, with no ore to process. Gold and platinum can be mined straight out of the ground in this form. The exam hint draws the contrast sharply: one metal can only remove oxygen from another metal's compound if it is the more reactive of the two.
keyPoints: The least reactive metals occur on their own, with no compound holding them.
They stay uncombined because their chemical stability stops them reacting with other substances.
Gold and platinum are mined straight out of the ground as metals.
No chemical extraction is needed for these metals because they hardly react.
A metal can only reduce another metal's compound if it is the more reactive of the two.

low.restatement: Some metals are so stable that they sit in the ground as elements, needing no chemistry to release them. Gold and platinum are the standard examples, dug up directly as metals.
low.analogy: A guest who joins nothing at a party is found standing alone; these metals refuse to combine, so they are found by themselves.
low.examPointer: Compare the two fates: reactive metals need ores and extraction, while gold and platinum are picked out as elements.

medium.restatement: Chemical stability explains native occurrence: an unreactive metal forms few compounds, so it lingers in the crust as the element itself. Gold and platinum are mined this way, while every more reactive metal must first be won from its ore by removing whatever it has combined with.
medium.analogy: Think of two neighbours: one joins every club on the street, like a reactive metal in compounds, while the other stays home alone, like gold sitting uncombined.
medium.examPointer: Reduction-direction questions hinge on reactivity: the reducing metal must outrank the metal in the compound, so quote the series before answering.

glossary.definition: A rock containing enough of a metal to make extracting that metal worthwhile.
Splitting a compound into its elements using electricity; one of the extraction routes.
The tall furnace in which iron is extracted from its ore by reduction with carbon monoxide.
The iron oxide ore used as the source of iron in the blast furnace.
The ore of aluminium, consisting of aluminium oxide.
An element present on its own rather than bonded into a compound.
The low tendency of a substance to react with other substances.

workedExample.prompt: a) Define an ore. b) Explain why extracting a metal from an oxide ore is called a reduction process. c) Name the ores of iron and aluminium, and explain why gold is often found as the uncombined element.
steps: a) An ore is a rock that contains enough of a metal to make extracting that metal worthwhile.
b) The metal is obtained by removing the oxygen from its oxide, and removal of oxygen is reduction.

c) Iron's ore is haematite (iron(III) oxide) and aluminium's is bauxite (aluminium oxide). Gold is so unreactive that it hardly forms compounds, so it lingers in the crust as the element itself and needs no chemical extraction.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) A rock worth mining for its metal. b) Oxygen is removed, which is reduction. c) Haematite and bauxite; gold is unreactive and occurs native.
